before: In the multi-agent debate paradigm, several LLM agents generate candidate answers and critique one another across one or more rounds. Representative studies illustrate both the potential and the limits of this design. For example, \citet{du2024multiagent_debate} report improved factuality and reasoning performance on the tasks they evaluate, whereas divergent prompting can mitigate convergence toward similar reasoning paths \citep{liang2024divergent_debate}. ReConcile provides another example by integrating heterogeneous models with confidence-weighted consensus \citep{chen2024reconcile}; answer consistency and degeneration nevertheless remain notable failure modes \citep{xiong2023inter_consistency}. Accordingly, adding more agents or debate rounds does not reliably boost QA performance; instead, the interaction rules, diversity of evidence, and aggregation procedure determine whether disagreement yields correction, inconsistency, or unnecessary computational cost.
after: In the multi-agent debate paradigm, several LLM agents generate candidate answers and critique one another across one or more rounds. Representative studies illustrate both the potential and the limits of this design. For example, \citet{du2024multiagent_debate} report improved factuality and reasoning performance on the tasks they evaluate, whereas divergent prompting can mitigate convergence toward similar reasoning paths \citep{liang2024divergent_debate}. ReConcile provides another example by integrating heterogeneous models with confidence-weighted consensus \citep{chen2024reconcile}; inter-model inconsistency and capability imbalance nevertheless remain important considerations \citep{xiong2023inter_consistency}. Accordingly, adding more agents or debate rounds does not reliably boost QA performance; instead, the interaction rules, diversity of evidence, and aggregation procedure determine whether disagreement yields correction, inconsistency, or unnecessary computational cost.

before:
With the rapid development of multi-agent ecosystems, interoperability barriers have arisen between agents developed by different vendors.
To address this issue, the industry has initiated efforts to standardize communication protocols. For example, Anthropic introduced the Model Context Protocol (MCP)
\citep{anthropic2024mcp}—dubbed the "USB-C of AI"—to standardise
the way agents connect to external tools and data sources.
Another example is Google's proposed Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol
\citep{google2025a2a}, which regulates horizontal peer-to-peer collaboration
among agents.
These standards are being gradually adopted by the open-source
community and the Linux Foundation, laying a foundation for heterogeneous
multi-agent QA systems.
after:
Industry initiatives address different parts of the interface problem.
Anthropic introduced the Model Context Protocol (MCP)
\citep{anthropic2024mcp} to standardise connections to external tools and data
sources. Google's Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol \citep{google2025a2a} supports
communication and task coordination between agents across frameworks and
vendors. These interfaces can support heterogeneous multi-agent QA systems.

after:
After decomposition, the system must assign sub-tasks to suitable agents.
For example, MetaGPT \citep{hong2024metagpt} organises agents through
predefined software-engineering roles, while AgentVerse
\citep{chen2024agentverse} recruits experts by generating task-specific
expertise descriptions and adjusts team composition using evaluation
feedback. These mechanisms guide which agents contribute to a task;
their scheduling efficiency requires separate evaluation.
